content: The World Health Organization (WHO) publication from 2017 outlines recommendations for newborn health, emphasizing evidence-based practices to improve outcomes for newborns and young infants. 1. Copyright and Licensing: The WHO permits the use, adaptation, and redistribution of its work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. The WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations must be licensed under equivalent Creative Commons terms. Translations must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation. 2. Guideline Development: WHO guidelines are developed using the highest international standards, ensuring transparency and minimizing bias. The process involves synthesizing and assessing evidence quality using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Evidence is categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low quality, and recommendations are classified as strong or conditional based on the balance of benefits and harms, feasibility, and other factors. 3. Immediate Newborn Care: Routine suctioning of the nose or mouth is not recommended for babies born through clear amniotic fluid who start breathing on their own (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Tracheal suctioning is not recommended for newborns born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid who start breathing on their own (strong recommendation, moderate-to-low-quality evidence). 4. Cord Clamping: Delayed cord clamping (1–3 minutes after birth) is recommended for all births while initiating essential newborn care (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Early cord clamping (<1 minute) is not recommended unless the newborn requires immediate resuscitation (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 5. Skin-to-Skin Contact and Breastfeeding: Newborns without complications should remain in skin-to-skin contact with their mothers during the first hour after birth to prevent hypothermia and promote breastfeeding (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). All newborns, including low-birth-weight infants who can breastfeed, should be put to the breast as soon as possible after birth when clinically stable (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). 6. Vitamin K Prophylaxis: All newborns should receive 1 mg of vitamin K intramuscularly after birth to prevent bleeding (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Newborns at high risk of bleeding (e.g., preterm infants, those exposed to maternal medications interfering with vitamin K) must also receive vitamin K (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 7. Postnatal Care: After an uncomplicated vaginal birth, mothers and newborns should remain in the health facility for at least 24 hours (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence). Postnatal care should include at least three additional contacts after the first 24 hours: on day 3, between days 7–14, and at 6 weeks postpartum (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence for newborn outcomes). 8. Home Visits: Home visits during the first week after birth are recommended to support the care of the mother and newborn (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence for newborn outcomes). 9. Exclusive Breastfeeding: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended from birth until 6 months of age. Mothers should receive counseling and support for breastfeeding during postnatal visits (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 10. Cord Care: Daily application of 4% chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord stump is recommended for newborns born at home in settings with high neonatal mortality. Clean, dry cord care is recommended in health facilities and low-mortality settings (strong situational recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 11. Keeping Newborns Warm: Bathing should be delayed for at least 24 hours after birth. If not culturally feasible, bathing should be delayed for at least 6 hours. Newborns should be dressed appropriately for the ambient temperature, with 1–2 layers more than adults and a hat. Mothers and babies should remain together in the same room 24 hours a day (strong situational recommendation). 12. Newborn Immunization: All infants should receive their first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, preferably within 24 hours (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Oral polio vaccine (birth dose) is recommended in polio-endemic countries and high-risk areas (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). In high tuberculosis-endemic areas, a single dose of BCG vaccine should be given to all infants (strong recommendation). 13. Management of Neonatal Illnesses: Neonates with signs of sepsis should be treated with ampicillin (or penicillin) and gentamicin for at least 10 days (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). In cases of critical illness, hospitalization is recommended after pre-referral treatment (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 14. Care for Preterm and Low-Birth-Weight Newborns: Preterm and low-birth-weight infants (>1200 g) who are clinically stable should be placed in skin-to-skin contact with their mothers soon after birth to prevent hypothermia. These recommendations aim to provide clear, evidence-based guidance for healthcare professionals, policymakers, and caregivers to improve newborn health outcomes globally.
